stem: Two isolated skeletal muscles from the same animal are stimulated with identical maximal tetanic trains and allowed to shorten against a very light constant load. Muscle X shortens three times faster than muscle Y, although the force per cross-sectional area is the same in both.
oneliner: Two isolated muscles + same maximal stimulation + light constant load + X shortens 3x faster than Y at equal force per area → which property accounts for the difference?
ask: Which property most likely explains the difference in maximum shortening velocity?

options.A: Larger amplitude of the action potentials
options.B: Higher frequency of the action potentials
options.D: Faster cross-bridge cycling by myosin ATPase

whyNot.A: Action potentials are **all-or-none**, and the stimulation was **identical**, so amplitude cannot differ
whyNot.B: Both received **identical trains**; and frequency changes **force** through summation, not the speed of cycling
whyNot.C: Phosphocreatine **buffers ATP** and prolongs work; it does not set how fast each head **cycles**
whyNot.E: This pump restores **membrane ion gradients** after action potentials; it does not drive **cross-bridge detachment**

answer: Rate of cross-bridge cycling (myosin ATPase activity)
why: At near-zero load, **shortening velocity depends on how fast myosin heads cycle**, which is set by the **myosin ATPase** isoform (fast-twitch versus slow-twitch). Force depends instead on the **number of cross-bridges** formed.
chain: Both release the same calcium and form the same force per area
Muscle X carries a fast myosin ATPase isoform
Its heads detach and reattach faster
Sarcomeres shorten at a higher velocity

idea.rule: Speed of shortening is set by myosin ATPase; force is set by the number of cross-bridges (and fiber size).
also: Type II fibers carry fast myosin ATPase and shorten faster than type I
Maximum velocity occurs at zero load, force is maximal at zero velocity (isometric)
Tetanic frequency raises force, not velocity
Slow type I fibers cycle slowly but resist fatigue through oxidative metabolism

stem: A 22-year-old man had deep lacerations that completely severed fibers of his thigh muscle in a car crash. Months later the gap has filled with a firm band of dense collagen, while the uninjured fibers on either side contract and relax normally when stimulated.
oneliner: 22M + severed thigh muscle fibers months ago, gap filled with dense collagen + surviving fibers contract and relax normally → which property is reduced?
ask: Which property of the healed muscle is most likely reduced?

options.E: Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

whyNot.A: The surviving fibers **contract normally**; collagen in the gap does not change how they **sustain tension**
whyNot.B: The stem says the surviving fibers **relax normally**
whyNot.D: Glycogen is stored inside **muscle fibers**, and the gap is filled with **collagen**, which does not alter glycogen handling
whyNot.E: The surviving fibers **contract and relax normally**, so their calcium release is intact

why: Skeletal muscle fibers regenerate poorly when completely severed, and the defect is filled with **dense collagenous scar** rather than new fibers. Collagen is **stiff and non-contractile**, so the muscle **loses extensibility** while the electrical and contractile properties of surviving fibers stay normal.
chain: Satellite cells cannot bridge the gap

idea.rule: Severed muscle heals by fibrosis: the scar adds stiffness but no contraction.
also: Satellite cells can regenerate small injuries but not a large gap
Contracture is the clinical result of fibrosis
Duchenne muscular dystrophy replaces muscle with fat and fibrous tissue
Ischemic injury (Volkmann contracture) also produces fibrosis

stem: An 8-year-old boy has extra unerupted teeth and shoulders that droop forward. Serum alkaline phosphatase is low, and calcium is normal.
oneliner: 8M + extra unerupted teeth + drooping shoulders + low serum ALP → which cell?
ask: Which bone cell does the low enzyme level point to?

whyNot.A: Osteoclasts resorb bone and make **acid phosphatase (TRAP)**, not alkaline phosphatase
whyNot.B: **Chondrocytes** build cartilage and are intact in this disease; endochondral bone is largely normal
whyNot.C: **Osteocytes** are buried mature cells that sense strain; they are not the ALP source
whyNot.D: **Fibroblasts** make collagen of soft tissue and are not the source of bone ALP

why: The picture is **cleidocranial dysplasia**, caused by loss of **RUNX2**, the master transcription factor for **osteoblast** differentiation. Osteoblasts release **alkaline phosphatase**, so fewer osteoblasts means **low serum ALP** with normal calcium.
chain: Serum ALP falls, calcium stays normal

idea.rule: Serum ALP mirrors osteoblast activity; calcium stays normal.
also: Paget disease: ALP high (osteoblast and osteoclast overactivity)
Osteomalacia: ALP high
Osteoblastic metastases (prostate): ALP high
Healing fracture: ALP rises
Osteoclast marker is TRAP

stem: A 35-year-old woman has a thin left calf after 6 weeks in a cast for a tibial fracture. Creatine kinase is normal, and a muscle biopsy shows no inflammation.
oneliner: 35F + 6 weeks of cast + thin calf + normal CK + no inflammation on biopsy → fibers?
ask: Which change in the muscle fibers is expected?

options.A: Fewer fibers, with the remaining fibers of normal size
options.B: Necrotic fibers with regeneration and inflammation
options.C: Smaller fibers; number unchanged; no necrosis
options.D: Fibers replaced by fat and fibrous tissue
options.E: Enlarged fibers from fluid and swelling

whyNot.A: **Loss of fibers** needs denervation death or necrosis; here the cells are still present
whyNot.B: **Necrosis with regeneration** raises CK and shows inflammation, which her biopsy lacks
whyNot.D: **Fat and fibrous replacement** is end-stage dystrophy, not 6 weeks of immobility
whyNot.E: **Enlarged fibers** would increase girth, but her calf is thin

answer: Fibers shrink from loss of contractile protein; number is unchanged
why: Without load, fibers **break down contractile protein faster than they make it**, so each fibre **shrinks** while the **number stays the same**. There is **no necrosis**, so **CK is normal**, and the change reverses with training.
chain: Muscle is unloaded in a cast
No necrosis, so CK stays normal

idea.rule: Disuse atrophy = smaller cells, same count, reversible; necrosis and fibrosis are different diseases.
also: Hypertrophy with training: bigger fibers, same count
Denervation atrophy: grouped small angular fibers
Duchenne: necrosis, high CK, later fibrofatty replacement
Aging: loss of fast type II fibers
Steroid myopathy: type II fiber atrophy

stem: A 50-year-old man has recurrent attacks in the big toe joint and a high serum urate. He starts a drug that blocks xanthine oxidase, the last enzyme of purine breakdown.
oneliner: 50M + recurrent big-toe attacks + hyperuricemia + drug that blocks xanthine oxidase → metabolites?
ask: Which set of changes occurs in his purine metabolites?

options.A: Urate up, hypoxanthine down, xanthine down
options.B: Urate unchanged, hypoxanthine down, xanthine up
options.C: Urate down, hypoxanthine down, xanthine down
options.D: Urate down, hypoxanthine up, xanthine up
options.E: Urate down, hypoxanthine up, xanthine down

whyNot.A: Urate is the **product** of the blocked enzyme, so it cannot rise
whyNot.B: Urate cannot stay level when its **last enzyme is blocked**, and hypoxanthine cannot drop
whyNot.C: **Everything cannot fall**; the substrates pile up behind the block
whyNot.E: The enzyme makes both steps (hypoxanthine to xanthine to urate), so **xanthine also accumulates**

answer: Urate falls; hypoxanthine and xanthine rise
why: Xanthine oxidase converts **hypoxanthine to xanthine to urate**. Blocking it **lowers urate** and makes the **more soluble** hypoxanthine and xanthine **back up** and be excreted, which is why crystals form less.
chain: Urate falls and is replaced by soluble metabolites

idea.rule: Block an enzyme: product falls, substrate rises behind it.
also: Allopurinol raises 6-MP and azathioprine levels (both cleared by xanthine oxidase)
Febuxostat gives the same pattern
Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase: acetaldehyde builds up
Carbidopa blocks peripheral dopa decarboxylase: more levodopa reaches the brain
Classic galactosemia: galactose-1-phosphate builds up behind the missing uridyltransferase

stem: Electron micrographs of an isolated skeletal muscle fiber are taken at rest and again at maximal contraction. A technician measures several distances in each sarcomere.
oneliner: Sarcomere at rest vs maximal contraction → which band keeps its length?

options.D: Sarcomere length (Z line to Z line)
options.E: Distance from M line to Z line

whyNot.B: The **H zone** (thick filaments only) shrinks as thin filaments slide inward
whyNot.C: The **I band** (thin filaments only) shrinks as Z lines approach thick filaments
whyNot.D: Whole **sarcomere length** falls because the Z lines move together
whyNot.E: The **M line to Z line distance** falls with the sarcomere, as both ends close in

why: Filaments **slide** past each other and do not shorten. The **A band equals the thick filament length**, so it is **constant**, while the **I band, H zone and sarcomere** all shorten.
chain: Myosin heads pull on thin filaments
Thin filaments slide over thick filaments
Z lines move closer; I band and H zone shrink
Thick filament length, the A band, is unchanged

idea.rule: Sliding filaments: A band constant; I band, H zone and sarcomere shorten.
also: Thick filaments = myosin; thin = actin
Z lines mark the sarcomere ends
M line is the midpoint of thick filaments
Cross-bridge cycling needs ATP and calcium
Rigor mortis: no ATP, filaments locked

stem: An isolated skeletal muscle fiber is placed in a bath with no calcium. When it is electrically stimulated, an action potential spreads along the T tubules, and cytosolic calcium still rises sharply and the fiber contracts.
oneliner: Skeletal fiber in calcium-free bath + stimulated → what links T-tubule depolarization to SR calcium release?
ask: Which step links T-tubule depolarization to calcium release?

options.A: Calcium entry through L-type channels triggering calcium-induced release
options.B: DHPR voltage sensing, directly opening the SR ryanodine receptor
options.C: Sodium leaving the sarcoplasmic reticulum through the T tubule
options.D: IP3 binding to its receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane
options.E: Na+/K+ pump activity on the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane

whyNot.A: That is the **cardiac** mechanism; here **no extracellular calcium** is present yet contraction occurs
whyNot.C: The SR **stores calcium, not sodium**, and releases calcium
whyNot.D: **IP3** signals smooth muscle and G-protein pathways, not skeletal excitation-contraction coupling
whyNot.E: The Na+/K+ pump restores resting gradients at the **plasma membrane** and does not release calcium

answer: Dihydropyridine receptor acting as a voltage sensor that mechanically opens RyR1
why: In **skeletal muscle**, the T-tubule **DHPR** acts as a **voltage sensor** and **physically opens the ryanodine receptor (RyR1)**, so it works **without extracellular calcium**. Calcium floods out of the SR and returns by **SERCA**.
chain: Action potential spreads down the T tubule
Calcium leaves the SR into the cytosol

idea.rule: Skeletal muscle: DHPR touches RyR1 (no extracellular calcium needed); cardiac muscle needs calcium entry first.
also: Cardiac: calcium-induced calcium release
Malignant hyperthermia: RyR1 mutation
Dantrolene blocks RyR1
SERCA pumps calcium back into the SR
